CHAPTER 2.1 · LEARNING AREA 2 · NOVEMBER

Limits and rates of change

Does Achilles ever catch up with the tortoise? What does a balance tend to if interest is added more and more often? How fast is a stone at exactly the moment it hits the ground? Behind all three questions is the limit, the tool with which differential calculus begins. You learn to find limits of sequences and functions and to turn an average into an instantaneous rate of change.

8 LESSONS3 UNITS1 LABPHYSICS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • investigate sequences of numbers and find their limit
  • read off the behaviour at infinity of polynomial functions from the highest term
  • calculate limits at a point and judge continuity intuitively
  • calculate and interpret average and instantaneous rates of change

UNIT 12 LESSONS

1Sequences of numbers and their limits

Achilles’ stages take 10 s, 1 s, 0.1 s, 0.01 s and so on. The sums 10; 11; 11.1; 11.11; … grow, but never get beyond $11.\overline{1}$. Calculated directly: Achilles gains 9 m per second, for 100 m he needs $\tfrac{100}{9} = 11.\overline{1}$ s. Infinitely many stages together take a finite time.

A sequence assigns a number $a_n$ to every natural number $n$, for example $a_n = \tfrac{n}{n+1}$: $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac23$, $\tfrac34$, … The terms come arbitrarily close to the number 1. We say: the sequence converges to the limit 1. Sequences without a limit are called divergent.

KEY POINT · LIMIT OF A SEQUENCE

$\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n = g$ means: for every tolerance, however small, from a certain $n$ onwards all further terms are closer to $g$ than this tolerance.

Null sequences: $\tfrac{1}{n} \to 0$, $\tfrac{c}{n^k} \to 0$ for $k > 0$

Fractions: divide numerator and denominator by the highest power of $n$: $\dfrac{n}{n + 1} = \dfrac{1}{1 + \frac1n} \to \dfrac{1}{1 + 0} = 1$

Explore digitally: in a spreadsheet put 1 in A1, the formula =A1+1 in A2 and drag it down, and =A1/(A1+1) in B1.

Divergent are, for example, $(-1)^n$ (jumps between $-1$ and $1$) and $n^2$ (grows beyond all bounds).

INTERACTIVE · ADDING INTEREST MORE AND MORE OFTEN

One euro, 100 % interest a year, but credited in smaller and smaller portions. The violet points are the sequence $\left(1 + \tfrac1n\right)^n$ for $n = 1$ to 40.

EXAMPLE 1 · LIMIT AND TOLERANCE

Find the limit of $a_n = \dfrac{3n + 2}{n}$. From which $n$ onwards do the terms differ from the limit by less than 0.01?

$a_n = 3 + \tfrac{2}{n} \to 3$. A difference $\tfrac{2}{n} < 0.01$ means $n > 200$.

Limit 3, from $n = 201$

EXAMPLE 2 · THE CIRCLE AS A LIMIT

A regular $n$-gon in a circle with radius 1 has the perimeter $U_n = 2n \cdot \sin\left(\tfrac{180^\circ}{n}\right)$. Calculate $U_6$, $U_{12}$ and $U_{96}$.

$U_6 = 6$, $U_{12} \approx 6.2117$, $U_{96} \approx 6.2821$.

The sequence tends to the circumference of the circle $2\pi \approx 6.2832$. Archimedes calculated in exactly this way with the 96-gon.

EXERCISES

Write down the first five terms of $a_n = \tfrac{1}{n^2}$ and give the limit.

$1$, $\tfrac14$, $\tfrac19$, $\tfrac{1}{16}$, $\tfrac{1}{25}$. Limit 0.

Find the limit: a) $\dfrac{2n - 1}{n}$   b) $5 + \dfrac{3}{n}$   c) $\dfrac{n + 4}{2n}$

a) $2$   b) $5$   c) $\tfrac12$

From which $n$ onwards is $\left|\tfrac{n}{n + 1} - 1\right| < 0.001$?

$1 - \tfrac{n}{n+1} = \tfrac{1}{n+1}$

$\tfrac{1}{n + 1} < 0.001$ means $n + 1 > 1000$: from $n = 1000$.

Convergent or divergent? a) $(-1)^n$   b) $\dfrac{(-1)^n}{n}$   c) $\dfrac{n^2}{n + 1}$

a) divergent, it jumps   b) convergent to 0   c) divergent, grows beyond all bounds

€1,000 earns 3 % interest a year. How much is in the account after one year if a share of the interest is credited yearly, monthly or daily? What value does the balance tend to?

Yearly €1,030, monthly $1000 \cdot \left(1 + \tfrac{0.03}{12}\right)^{12} \approx 1030.42$ €, daily about €1,030.45. Limit $1000 \cdot \mathrm{e}^{0.03} \approx 1030.45$ €: adding interest more often brings no more than 45 cents.

$4 + \tfrac1n \to 4$

UNIT 23 LESSONS

2Limits of functions and continuity

$f(x) = -2x^3 + 50x^2 + 100$ is still 3100 at $x = 10$, but already $-1\,499\,900$ at $x = 100$. Factoring out shows why: $f(x) = x^3 \left(-2 + \tfrac{50}{x} + \tfrac{100}{x^3}\right)$. The bracket tends to $-2$, so $f(x) \to -\infty$ for $x \to \infty$. The term with the highest power wins.

For functions you ask what happens to $f(x)$ when $x$ gets larger and larger or approaches a point $x_0$. To do this you substitute values that are closer and closer to $x_0$, from the left and from the right. If both sides agree with the function value, you can draw the graph there without lifting your pen: the function is continuous.

KEY POINT · BEHAVIOUR AT INFINITY AND CONTINUITY

For $f(x) = a_n x^n + \ldots + a_0$, $a_n x^n$ decides: $n$ even: both ends like the sign of $a_n$ · $n$ odd: for $a_n > 0$ from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$, for $a_n < 0$ the other way round.

$\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} f(x) = g$ if $f(x)$ tends to $g$ when approached from the left and from the right.

$f$ is continuous at $x_0$ if $\lim\limits_{x \to x_0} f(x) = f(x_0)$.

Test values: substitute $x_0 \pm 0.1$, $x_0 \pm 0.01$, $x_0 \pm 0.001$, ideally with the table of the graphing calculator.

Cancelling helps: with “$\tfrac{0}{0}$” factorise the numerator. Polynomial functions are continuous everywhere.

INTERACTIVE · STEP BY STEP TO THE LIMIT

Choose a function and a direction. With every step the values move ten times closer to the point or ten times further out.

EXAMPLE 3 · BEHAVIOUR AT INFINITY

Describe the behaviour of $f(x) = -0.5x^4 + 3x^3 + x$ for $x \to \pm\infty$.

Highest term $-0.5x^4$: even exponent, negative factor.

$f(x) \to -\infty$ for $x \to \infty$ and for $x \to -\infty$

EXAMPLE 4 · A HOLE IN THE GRAPH

Calculate $\lim\limits_{x \to 2} \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$. Is the function continuous at 2?

$\dfrac{(x - 2)(x + 2)}{x - 2} = x + 2$ for $x \neq 2$: limit 4.

At $x = 2$ it is not defined, so it is not continuous there. If you set $f(2) = 4$, it becomes continuous.

EXERCISES

Describe the behaviour for $x \to \pm\infty$: a) $2x^3 - x$   b) $-x^4 + 5x^2$   c) $3 - x$

a) $-\infty$ on the left, $+\infty$ on the right   b) both ends $-\infty$   c) $+\infty$ on the left, $-\infty$ on the right

Find $\lim\limits_{x \to 3} \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$ with test values at 2.9, 2.99, 3.01 and 3.1.

Values 5.9, 5.99, 6.01, 6.1: limit 6.

Calculate $\lim\limits_{x \to 1} \dfrac{x^2 + x - 2}{x - 1}$ by cancelling.

$x^2 + x - 2 = (x - 1)(x + 2)$: limit $1 + 2 = 3$.

$f(x) = x^2$ for $x \le 1$ and $f(x) = 2x + a$ for $x > 1$. For which $a$ is $f$ continuous?

Both parts must have the same value at $x = 1$.

$1 = 2 + a$: $a = -1$

Find by dividing by the highest power of $x$: a) $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{3x^2 + 1}{x^2 + 2}$   b) $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{2x + 1}{x^2 + 1}$. What does this mean for the graphs?

a) $\dfrac{3 + \frac{1}{x^2}}{1 + \frac{2}{x^2}} \to 3$: horizontal asymptote $y = 3$.   b) $\dfrac{\frac2x + \frac{1}{x^2}}{1 + \frac{1}{x^2}} \to 0$: the asymptote is the $x$-axis. More on this in chapter 4.1.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is $\lim\limits_{x \to 2} \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$?

$x + 2 \to 4$

$f(x) = x^2$ for $x \le 1$, $f(x) = 2x + a$ for $x > 1$. For which $a$ is $f$ continuous?

$1 = 2 + a$

$f(x) = -3x^5 + x$ for $x \to \infty$:

Odd exponent, negative factor.

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3Average and instantaneous rate of change

A stone falls; after $t$ seconds it has fallen about $s(t) = 5t^2$ metres. From the first to the third second it falls $45 - 5 = 40$ m, on average $\tfrac{40}{2} = 20$ m/s. How fast is it at exactly $t = 2$? On $[2, 2 + h]$ the average is $\dfrac{5(2 + h)^2 - 20}{h} = 20 + 5h$. The smaller $h$, the closer to 20 m/s.

The average rate of change compares two moments: the change divided by the time taken. In the graph it is the gradient of the secant through two points. If you let the second moment move closer and closer to the first, it becomes the instantaneous rate of change, the gradient of the tangent. That is the idea of the derivative.

KEY POINT · RATES OF CHANGE

Average rate of change (difference quotient) on $[a, b]$: $\dfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$, the gradient of the secant

Instantaneous rate of change at the point $x_0$: $\lim\limits_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0)}{h}$, the gradient of the tangent

Unit: unit of $f$ per unit of $x$, for example m/s, °C/h or € per item.

In everyday life: average speed and speedometer, average and instantaneous growth rate, inflow per minute, cost of one additional item.

h-method: multiply out $f(x_0 + h)$, subtract $f(x_0)$, cancel $h$, and only then set $h = 0$.

INTERACTIVE · FROM SECANT TO TANGENT

Drag the point $P$ and make the distance $h$ smaller and smaller. The green step shows $h$ and $f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0)$; the secant turns into the tangent.

EXAMPLE 5 · TEMPERATURE IN THE MORNING

$T(t) = 12 + 3t - 0.25t^2$ is the temperature in °C, $t$ in hours after 8 o’clock. Calculate the average rate of change from 8 to 12 o’clock and the instantaneous one at 9 o’clock.

$\tfrac{T(4) - T(0)}{4} = \tfrac{20 - 12}{4} = 2$ °C/h.

$\dfrac{T(1 + h) - T(1)}{h} = \dfrac{2.5h - 0.25h^2}{h} = 2.5 - 0.25h \to$ 2.5 °C/h at 9 o’clock

EXAMPLE 6 · THE FALLING STONE

How fast is the stone with $s(t) = 5t^2$ after 2 seconds?

$\dfrac{5(4 + 4h + h^2) - 20}{h} = \dfrac{20h + 5h^2}{h} = 20 + 5h \to 20$

20 m/s, that is 72 km/h

EXERCISES

Calculate the average rate of change of $f(x) = x^2$ on $[1, 3]$ and on $[1, 1.1]$.

$\tfrac{9 - 1}{2} = 4$ and $\tfrac{1.21 - 1}{0.1} = 2.1$

At 6 o’clock the river is at 1.20 m, at 10 o’clock at 0.80 m. What is the average rate of change? What does the sign mean?

$\tfrac{0.80 - 1.20}{4} = -0.1$ m/h: the level falls by 10 cm per hour.

Use the h-method to find the instantaneous rate of change of $f(x) = x^2$ at the point $x_0 = 3$.

$\dfrac{(3 + h)^2 - 9}{h} = 6 + h \to 6$

A town has $N(t) = 1000 \cdot 1.02^t$ inhabitants (in thousands, $t$ in years). Calculate the average rate of change in the first 10 years and estimate the instantaneous one at $t = 0$ with $h = 0.001$.

$\tfrac{N(10) - N(0)}{10} \approx 21.9$ thousand per year. At $t = 0$: $\tfrac{N(0.001) - 1000}{0.001} \approx 19.8$ thousand per year.

A stone falls from a height of 45 m, $s(t) = 5t^2$. When and at what speed does it hit the ground?

$5t^2 = 45$, $t = 3$ s. $\dfrac{5(3 + h)^2 - 45}{h} = 30 + 5h \to 30$: 30 m/s, that is 108 km/h.

The average rate of change of $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 2]$?

$\tfrac{4 - 0}{2}$

The instantaneous rate of change of $f(x) = x^2$ at $x_0 = 3$?

$6 + h \to 6$

$T(t) = 12 + 3t - 0.25t^2$: how fast is the temperature rising at $t = 1$?

$2.5 - 0.25h \to 2.5$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Find $\lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{5n - 3}{n}$.

$5 - \tfrac3n \to 5$

Connecting with Year 11: a bacterial culture doubles every hour, $N(t) = 100 \cdot 2^t$. What is the average rate of change in the third hour? Why is it larger than in the first?

$\tfrac{N(3) - N(2)}{1} = 800 - 400 = 400$ bacteria per hour, in the first only 100. Exponential growth gets faster and faster.

With the 96-gon Archimedes showed that $3\tfrac{10}{71} < \pi < 3\tfrac17$. Check the bounds with the calculator and compare with $\tfrac{U_{96}}{2}$ from example 2.

$3\tfrac{10}{71} \approx 3.14085$, $3\tfrac17 \approx 3.14286$, $\pi \approx 3.14159$ lies in between. $\tfrac{U_{96}}{2} \approx 3.14103$; the inscribed 96-gon is still a little too small.

A cyclist sets off: $s(t) = 0.5t^2$ for $0 \le t \le 4$, after that $s(t) = 8 + 4(t - 4)$ (in m and s). Show that $s$ is continuous at $t = 4$. Does the speed jump there, or does it change smoothly?

Both parts give $s(4) = 8$: continuous. Left: $\dfrac{8 - 0.5(4 - h)^2}{h} = 4 - 0.5h \to 4$, right: 4 m/s. No jump, the speed changes smoothly.

EXCURSIONPHILOSOPHY AND HISTORY

Zeno’s paradox

In the 5th century BC the Greek philosopher Zeno of Elea claimed that the fastest runner could never catch up with the slowest: every time he gets to where the slow one was, the slow one is already a little further on. The stages never end, so the chase never ends either.

For more than two thousand years philosophers argued about where the mistake lies. The answer of mathematics: infinitely many time spans can add up to a finite length. $10 + 1 + 0.1 + 0.01 + \ldots = 11.\overline{1}$ is the limit of a sequence of sums. Only with the concept of a limit in the 19th century was this put on a sound footing.

Source: Handed down by Aristotle, “Physics”, Book VI, chapter 9 (239b). Overview: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Zeno’s Paradoxes”.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

SEQUENCES

Divide by the highest power of $n$, drop null sequences.

$\dfrac{3n + 2}{n} = 3 + \dfrac2n \to 3$

AT INFINITY

The highest term $a_n x^n$ decides.

$-0.5x^4 + \ldots$: both ends $-\infty$

AT A POINT

Approach from the left and from the right, resolve “$\tfrac00$” by cancelling.

$\dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2} \to 4$ for $x \to 2$

CONTINUOUS

Limit equals function value: draw without lifting the pen.

$x^2$ and $2x - 1$ meet at $(1, 1)$

RATES OF CHANGE

Average: gradient of the secant · instantaneous: limit for $h \to 0$, gradient of the tangent

$s(t) = 5t^2$: $20 + 5h \to 20$ m/s
